question.prompt: Let \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) denote the greatest integer less than or equal to \(x.\) How many real numbers \(x\) satisfy the equation \(x^2+10{,}000\lfloor x\rfloor=10{,}000x?\)

solutions.title: Count one solution per floor interval
solutions.explanation:
The useful observation is that \(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\), the fractional part of \(x\), always lies in \([0,1)\). Rearranging the equation gives
\[
x^2=10{,}000\bigl(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr),
\]
so every solution satisfies \(0\le x^2<10{,}000\). Consequently,
\[
-100<x<100.
\]
Define \(P(x)=10{,}000x-x^2\). The original equation is equivalent to
\[
P(x)=10{,}000\lfloor x\rfloor.
\]
We will count solutions separately on the intervals \([k,k+1)\), where \(k=-100,-99,\ldots,99\). On each such interval, the right side is the constant \(10{,}000k\).

First, \(P\) is strictly increasing throughout \([-100,100]\). Indeed, if \(-100\le u<v\le100\), then
\[
P(v)-P(u)=(v-u)(10{,}000-u-v)>0,
\]
since both factors are positive. Thus each interval contains at most one solution.

At its left endpoint,
\[
P(k)=10{,}000k-k^2\le10{,}000k.
\]
At its excluded right endpoint,
\[
P(k+1)=10{,}000k+10{,}000-(k+1)^2.
\]
Because \(P\) is continuous and strictly increasing, it reaches \(10{,}000k\) within \([k,k+1)\) exactly when
\[
P(k+1)>10{,}000k,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
(k+1)^2<10{,}000
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-101<k<99.
\]
Among the candidate integers, these are precisely \(k=-100,-99,\ldots,98\). Each contributes one solution. This includes \(x=0\) at the left endpoint of \([0,1)\); the half-open intervals ensure that no solution is counted twice.

Therefore the number of solutions is
\[
98-(-100)+1=\boxed{199},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
